key_concept: Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that lie outside the bacterial chromosome (extrachromosomal) and replicate on their own (autonomously), which is why they are used as cloning vectors.
steps: Recall the definition: a plasmid is a small, usually circular, double-stranded DNA found in bacteria (and some yeasts) in addition to the main chromosomal DNA.
Statement I: Plasmids carry their own origin of replication (ori). This lets them replicate independently of the chromosome. So they are autonomously replicating, and Statement I is correct.
Statement II: Plasmids exist separately from the bacterial nucleoid (chromosomal) DNA in the cytoplasm. So they are extrachromosomal, and Statement II is correct.
Link to rDNA technology: because of the ori, any foreign DNA linked to a plasmid is copied along with it. Copy number can range from 1 to many per cell, so plasmids make good vectors (e.g., pBR322).
Both statements are correct, so the answer is Option (1).
final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
why_not_others: Options (3) and (4) each reject one statement. However, autonomous replication (due to ori) and extrachromosomal location are both defining features of plasmids, so neither can be marked incorrect. Option (2) is plainly wrong.
common_trap: Students may think that if plasmids replicate using host enzymes, they are not 'autonomous'. In fact, autonomy refers to replication independent of the chromosome, controlled by the plasmid's own ori.
time_saving_tip: Remember the one-line textbook definition: 'Plasmids are autonomously replicating circular extrachromosomal DNA.' It covers both statements at once.
